interest:
I am interested in AI, machine learning, large language models (LLMs), large
multimodal models (LMMs), foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation,
research agents, and automated scientific discovery methods that can be
useful for astronomy and astrophysics.

Prioritize papers that could help with:
1. JWST imaging/spectroscopy analysis, especially high-redshift galaxies,
   AGN, and little red dots
2. astronomical source classification, anomaly detection, morphology,
   deblending, photometric redshifts, SED fitting, spectral fitting, or
   uncertainty estimation
3. multimodal models that combine images, spectra, catalogs, tables, text, or
   literature
4. LLM agents for literature review, data analysis, coding, scientific
   workflows, or reproducible research
5. methods that could transfer to large survey data from JWST, Roman, Euclid,
   Rubin/LSST, HST, ALMA, or multi-wavelength catalogs

Deprioritize generic NLP, chatbots, robotics, games, social media, medicine,
finance, or benchmark-only papers unless the method clearly transfers to
astronomical research workflows.

papers.title: Safe Domain Adaptation for Physics: Overcoming Nuisances, Label Shifts, and Simulation Priors
papers.authors: Ivan Kharuk (1 and 2) ((1) Institute for Nuclear Research of the Russian Academy of Sciences, (2) Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology)
papers.subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG) ; Instrumentation and Methods for Astrophysics (astro-ph.IM); Data Analysis, Statistics and Probability (physics.data-an)
papers.abstract: Domain adaptation is widely used to make neural networks trained on simulations applicable to experimental data. Its premise is that the two domains differ only in nuisances, and that the quantity of interest is distributed identically in both. In physics neither assumption holds: simulations can be wrong about the physics, and the distribution of the target quantity - an energy spectrum, a redshift distribution - is often the measurement itself. We study the consequences of such mismatches on a toy air-shower benchmark in which a detector-response nuisance, a physical simulation shift, and an energy-spectrum shift can be switched on separately or together. Standard adversarial adaptation handles the conditional shifts, but once the two spectra differ it aligns them, replacing an uncontrolled bias by one anchored on the simulation prior. We present adaptive domain adaptation, which reweights the simulated events so as to focus domain adaptation on the genuine physical mismatch alone. Since the predicted spectrum depends on model training configuration, we provide a label-free model selection rule for selecting the near-the-best operation point.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses domain adaptation for physics data, including label shifts and simulation priors, which is relevant to applying ML models trained on simulations to real astronomical observations like JWST data. The focus on handling distribution shifts and model selection without labels is useful for photometric redshifts or SED fitting.
papers.Short digest: This paper tackles the problem of adapting neural networks trained on simulations to experimental data when the simulations are imperfect and the target quantity (e.g., an energy spectrum or redshift distribution) is itself the measurement. The main idea is 'adaptive domain adaptation,' which reweights simulated events to focus adaptation on genuine physical mismatches rather than aligning distributions that should differ. This matters for astronomy because models trained on simulated galaxy spectra or images often need to be applied to real JWST data where the true redshift distribution is unknown. A concrete workflow could be adapting a source classifier trained on simulated high-redshift galaxies to real JWST photometry, with the redshift distribution as the target. A key caveat is that the method assumes the simulation prior is not completely wrong, and the label-free model selection rule should be tested on your specific dataset before trusting the results.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the toy benchmark setup is described clearly enough to map to astronomical domain shifts (e.g., detector noise vs. physical model errors).
Look for details on the label-free model selection rule and whether it requires any validation data or assumptions.
Examine how the reweighting is computed and whether it scales to high-dimensional inputs like images or spectra.

papers.title: Metrics That Write Themselves: Evolving an Evaluator from Its Own Blind Spots
papers.authors: Xing Zhang , Yanwei Cui , Guanghui Wang , Zhihao Lin , Peiyang He
papers.subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI) ; Computation and Language (cs.CL); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
papers.abstract: Agents improve quickly against a reliable automatic metric and stall without one, and the applications that need them most, report generation among them, are the ones nobody knows how to score. Can the metric write itself? Saying what makes an answer good is hard; pointing at something wrong with one is easier, so the metric we evolve is a pool of small Python operators that each flag a candidate for one named defect, or abstain, and vote. Asking a model for operators directly does not work: 183 candidates realise only 96 distinct behaviours, from one narrow region of an enormous space. EvalCEGAR instead borrows counterexample-guided abstraction refinement from program verification. It reads the pool as an abstraction and searches for a collision, two answers the operators score identically, one correct and one not. That pair, not a prompt, is the authoring request, and when a collision defeats every attempt the loop widens what an operator may read rather than resampling. On MBPP+ and HumanEval+, a sandbox whose hidden unit tests give exact ground truth, the loop writes a 55-line operator that closes 15.4% of the gap between flagging nothing and a perfect filter on 428 unseen tasks (+0.0065, p=0.0010) at a quarter of our best hand-written operator's flags. On the benchmark it never saw it matches that operator's effect exactly on a third of the flags. Six of eight runs admit such an operator and all six help out of sample; our 15 hand-written operators applied together as one filter lose accuracy. An LLM judge on the same information ties that delta on a nearly disjoint set of candidates, and charges a model call per candidate forever where the operator charges none.
papers.Reasons for match: Directly addresses automated metric generation for agents, which is relevant to building research agents for astronomy. The idea of evolving an evaluator from blind spots could transfer to automated scientific discovery workflows where scoring model outputs is hard.
papers.Short digest: This paper asks whether an automatic metric for evaluating agent outputs can be written by the agent itself, since hand-writing good metrics is hard. The main idea is EvalCEGAR, which uses counterexample-guided abstraction refinement to evolve a pool of small Python operators that flag defects, by searching for pairs of correct and incorrect answers that the current operators cannot distinguish. This matters for astronomy because it offers a way to automatically create evaluation metrics for complex outputs like source catalogs or spectral fits, where defining correctness is difficult. A concrete workflow could be evolving a metric to score LLM-generated summaries of JWST data analysis results. However, the method requires a sandbox with hidden ground truth (like unit tests) to guide evolution, which may be hard to construct for many astronomical tasks.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check whether the evolved operators are interpretable or just black-box functions
Look for details on how the collision search is implemented and its computational cost
See if the method is tested on any domain beyond code generation, or if it requires a reliable ground-truth oracle

papers.title: Teach a Molmo2Fish: Towards interactive fish tracking with natural language guidance
papers.authors: Kai Van Brunt (1), Justin Kay (1), Sara Beery (1) ((1) Massachusetts Institute of Technology)
papers.abstract: Computer vision is increasingly used to automate recognition tasks in large ecological datasets, but more complex tasks such as multi-object tracking continue to pose challenges. As researchers seek to incorporate vision models in ecology workflows, various lines of research have explored how to make imperfect predictions useful through human-in-the-loop processes. We propose a new approach to working with imperfect tracking predictions through an interactive prediction correction workflow taking place as a conversation with a multimodal large language model, which we tailor to a sonar fish tracking dataset as an initial proof of concept. We investigate the performance of the tool, Molmo2Fish, across guided and unguided tasks, correcting its own predicted tracks and external tracks. We find that Molmo2Fish achieves high performance on fish tracking and track correction tasks, but there is still much room to improve on incorporating natural language guidance. The code and data are publicly available at this https URL .
papers.Reasons for match: Interactive fish tracking with natural language guidance, which could transfer to astronomical object tracking or human-in-the-loop analysis. The multimodal LLM approach is relevant to combining vision and language.
papers.Short digest: This paper explores using a multimodal LLM to correct tracking predictions through conversation, applied to sonar fish data. It shows high performance on correcting tracks but notes room for improvement in language guidance. For astronomy, this could help with interactive analysis of moving objects in survey data. A workflow might be using such a tool to correct asteroid tracks in images. The caveat is that the dataset is sonar, not optical, and the method is a proof of concept.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the method requires a pre-trained multimodal model that can handle astronomical images
Look for details on how the language guidance is incorporated and its limitations
Inspect whether the approach could scale to large survey datasets

papers.title: Can a Lightweight Multimodal Model Estimate LLM Reasoning Performance? A Study for Compute-Optimal Document Inference
papers.abstract: Uniformly allocating inference reasoning budgets to LLMs is expensive and prone to over-thinking penalties; especially in document tasks where visual layouts drive complexity. To address this, we introduce BudgetDoc, the first multimodal benchmark providing explicit supervision for model-budget-performance trade-offs across three document tasks. Using BudgetDoc, we train DRB (Document-Reasoning Balancer), an approx. 1B-parameter pre-flight estimator (SigLIP-2 + Qwen3-0.6B) that predicts ordinal model performance across budget levels, achieving a 0.753 weighted F1. When dynamically allocating reasoning budgets across five frontier models and three datasets, DRB matches or improves F1 scores compared to always-maximum-budget baselines in 9 of 15 configurations while drastically reducing cost. Finally, preliminary evaluations demonstrate DRB's potential to generalize to cross-model selection.
papers.Reasons for match: Estimates LLM reasoning performance to allocate compute, which could transfer to optimizing inference for astronomical document analysis. The multimodal aspect is relevant to handling figures and tables in papers.
papers.Short digest: This paper introduces a benchmark and a small model to predict LLM performance across reasoning budgets for document tasks. It shows that dynamic budget allocation can match or improve accuracy while reducing cost. For astronomy, this could help decide how much compute to spend on analyzing papers or data summaries. A workflow might be using such an estimator to allocate resources for literature review agents. The caveat is that the benchmark is on document QA, not scientific data, and the model is small and task-specific.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the benchmark includes any scientific documents or tables
Look for details on the features used by the estimator (e.g., layout, text length)
Inspect whether the method can generalize to different LLM families and tasks

papers.title: CTIFoundry: An Agent-Native Corpus Scaffold for Cyber Threat Intelligence
papers.authors: Yutong Cheng , Changze Li , Qian Cui , Wei Ding , Lingzhi Wang , Yan Chen , Peng Gao
papers.abstract: Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) is increasingly consumed not by human analysts but by LLM agents that compose multi-step investigations at query time. The harness side of this shift has matured rapidly (planning loops, tool protocols, context management), but the corpus side has not: threat reports and vulnerability databases are still packaged for retrieval-augmented generation, as opaque chunks behind an embedding index. We argue that this substrate, not model capability, is the bottleneck on agentic CTI investigation, and present CTIFoundry, an agent-native corpus scaffold. At build time, CTIFoundry materializes the latent structure of a CTI corpus: a deterministic ontology graph over four authoritative knowledge bases (CVE, CWE, CAPEC, ATT&CK) whose official cross-references become typed, traversable edges; a span-grounded report layer whose canonical, alias-resolved cross-vendor entities index provenance-carrying chunks; and hybrid dense+lexical retrieval surfaces. At query time this structure is exposed through seven typed tools and three procedural skills mounted on a stock open-source agent harness. On the public CTIConnect benchmark, swapping only the action surface lifts the identically-harnessed agent by +0.19 to +0.28 overall F1 across a four-model, two-provider panel: a small model on CTIFoundry surpasses a flagship on the flat substrate, and the gain is not bought with search effort, since on both Claude models the scaffolded agent is more accurate at roughly half the tool calls. An ablation attributes it: typed structure carries the larger share, procedural skills convert structure into discipline, and the two compose super-additively, because skills bind only to structure that exists.
papers.Reasons for match: Agent-native corpus scaffold for cyber threat intelligence, which could transfer to building research agents for astronomy literature. The ontology and retrieval structure is relevant to scientific knowledge management.
papers.Short digest: This paper argues that the bottleneck in agentic cyber threat intelligence is the corpus structure, not model capability. It proposes a scaffold that materializes ontology graphs and typed tools for retrieval. For astronomy, this could help build agents that navigate literature and databases like ADS or SIMBAD. A workflow might be creating an agent that queries multiple astronomical databases with typed tools. The caveat is that the ontology is specific to cybersecurity and would need re-engineering for astronomy.
Full-text inspection checklist: Check if the ontology and tools are domain-specific or could be adapted
Look for details on the retrieval surfaces and their scalability
Inspect whether the gains are due to structure or the specific benchmark
